Triggers.value: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I can no longer trust my own body

vignette:
Imani sits rigidly in the chair, her hands clenched in the lap of her stiff work trousers. At forty-two, she has built a new life for herself, but the architecture of that life feels fragile, ready to collapse at any moment. The trauma is now years in the past, a continent away, but it lives in the air she breathes. It happened on a day of suffocating humidity, the kind where the air is thick and smells of damp earth and coming rain. That smell is something she can still conjure, or rather, it conjures itself without her permission. A whiff from a potted plant after watering, the scent of a summer shower on hot asphalt, and she is back in that small, windowless room. When she speaks of it, her voice is flat, distant. The memory feels like it belongs to someone else, a story she read or a film she watched about a woman who looked like her. She finds it hard to believe it actually happened to her; the cruelty was so absolute, so extreme, that it resists reality.

In that room, he was always close. His name was Joseph, and the sound of his name, or even similar-sounding names like Joe or Joshua, can stop her breath. The core of the horror was his proximity, the feeling of being unable to move as he stood over her. Now, this fear has metastasized into her daily life at the factory. The floor is crowded, the aisles between the humming machinery narrow. When a coworker brushes past her, even accidentally, her body reacts before her mind has a chance to process the innocence of the touch. A jolt of pure terror, a surge of adrenaline that makes her muscles lock and her heart hammer against her ribs. She feels betrayed by her own physiology, convinced she can no longer trust her own body to know the difference between a real threat and a colleague trying to get by. The ordinary sounds of the factory—the sudden clang of dropped metal, the high-pitched whine of a conveyor belt starting up—make her jump so violently she’s nearly dropped her tools.

This sense of pervasive threat is not confined to work. Some mornings, she wakes to find the air outside her window heavy and grey, the humidity so thick it feels like a blanket. On these days, the simple act of walking to the bus stop becomes an ordeal. The oppressive weight of the atmosphere presses in on her, mirroring the feeling of that small, windowless room, and she is certain that something terrible is about to happen again. To navigate this world she now perceives as fundamentally dangerous, Imani has developed a rigid set of rules. Each morning, she applies a thick layer of makeup, a mask that feels like armour. It hides the fatigue in her eyes, but more importantly, it feels like a barrier between her and the world. She never wears dresses, especially not the simple cotton kind she was wearing that day. The sight of them in a store window is enough to make her cross the street. Her most consuming strategy, however, is the relentless battle against silence and stillness. At home, the television is always on, loud enough to fill every corner of her small apartment. She cannot simply sit; she must be cleaning, cooking, sorting, anything to keep her mind occupied, to prevent the images and sensations from finding a foothold. The effort is exhausting, but the alternative—the quiet in which the memories begin to replay—is unbearable.

This constant vigilance has hollowed out her life. At night, she lies in bed not relaxing but listening, monitoring every creak of the floorboards, every distant siren, for any sound that might mean someone is entering her home. She has come to believe she is no longer the capable, resilient woman who survived and escaped. That woman, she feels, is gone. In her place is this fragile creature who flinches at shadows and whose body is a traitor. The final straw that brought her to therapy was a formal warning from her shift supervisor. Her startle responses and moments of dissociation had led to several mistakes, slowing down the production line. The threat of losing her job, the one thing that provides her with structure and independence, made her realize she could not go on like this. She is here now, terrified that she is permanently broken, but clinging to a desperate hope that she might one day feel safe inside her own skin again.
